title: Park Safety

jokes.text: The hummingbird lottery: winner gets to refill bird feeders, not win a hummingbird
jokes.setup: Leslie announces a 'hummingbird lottery,' which implies something exciting or valuable
jokes.punchline: The prize is just refilling hummingbird feeders — a chore disguised as a prize by Leslie's genuine enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: Works because it immediately establishes Leslie's relentless optimism — she genuinely thinks this is a fun reward. The subversion of lottery expectations is clean and quick. Deeply character-specific; only Leslie would frame a chore as a prize.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: They just win the chore of refilling feeders

jokes.text: Scientifically, hummingbirds are the world's cutest animals. I mean, they're so small. And they have tiny beaks. And they only eat sugar water. I mean, what beats that?
jokes.setup: Leslie declares hummingbirds are scientifically the cutest animals and builds a case
jokes.punchline: The 'scientific' claim is backed only by childlike observations ('tiny beaks,' 'sugar water') delivered with total conviction
jokes.explanation: The word 'scientifically' doing heavy lifting against non-scientific reasoning is very Leslie. The list of endearing qualities is funny in its simplicity. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Hummingbirds are scientifically the cutest animal. It's been proven. Their little wings go so fast they're basically just a blur of adorableness, and their beaks are like tiny swords of cuteness.

jokes.text: Come on. Baby monkeys in diapers? Yeah. They do.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks 'what beats that?' about hummingbirds eating sugar water
jokes.punchline: She immediately concedes baby monkeys in diapers are cuter, undermining her entire argument
jokes.explanation: Tight misdirection: she poses a rhetorical question with confident authority, then immediately and cheerfully concedes. The specificity of 'baby monkeys in diapers' is perfectly absurd. Economical and well-structured. One of the stronger jokes in the cold open.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. Baby monkeys in diapers. You win.

jokes.text: No, I always write my own name. But just to be safe, I do add 20 extra 'Jerry's.
jokes.setup: Tom is about to reveal how he avoids the lottery, implying he cheats somehow
jokes.punchline: He admits he adds 20 extra slips with Jerry's name — casually confessing to systematic rigging
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's first big laugh. The beat before — the camera cutaway to the talking head — is a perfect structural device. Tom's casual, unapologetic confession ('just to be safe') reveals both his laziness and his cruelty toward Jerry in one line. Highly quotable, strong character integration, and the '20 extra' specificity is key. One of the episode's standout moments.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, everyone, we need someone to handle the hummingbird feeders this week.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Not me. I'm allergic to nature.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'd rather eat glass.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Child, please.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't do birds. They're plotting something.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I would, but I have that... thing.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I'll do it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Really? That's so nice of you, Jerry!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Well, I always seem to—

dialogue.speaker: Everyone
dialogue.line: Great, thanks Jerry!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: —end up with the worst jobs anyway.

jokes.text: I thought Freddy Spaghetti OD'd. / No. That's Mr. Funny Noodle. And he didn't OD, his drummer shot him.
jokes.setup: Leslie announces a children's entertainer named Freddy Spaghetti for the concert series
jokes.punchline: Tom confuses him with Mr. Funny Noodle, whose fate — being shot by his drummer — is delivered as a mundane correction
jokes.explanation: Exceptional dark absurdist comedy. The double escalation (OD → being shot by drummer) delivered as a bland factual correction is perfectly structured. The names 'Freddy Spaghetti' and 'Mr. Funny Noodle' are inspired. Leslie's 'Oh' response — treating this as normal — is the ideal reaction beat. High quotability, very original.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hey Jerry, I heard about your bad luck. That's rough, man. I'm really sorry to hear that.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Thanks, Tom. I appreciate that.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, no problem. Hey, you know what? I'm gonna go stand over there. Far away from you. Because I don't want any of that bad luck rubbing off on me.

jokes.text: Maybe he fell into the toilet. / Remember when he fell into the toilet?
jokes.setup: The team notices Jerry hasn't returned from filling the bird feeders
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately suggests Jerry fell into a toilet — and someone confirms this has happened before
jokes.explanation: A quick character bit that efficiently builds the Jerry mythology. The confirmation that it's happened before elevates it from a random insult to a running gag with history.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I have a system. I only play numbers that have never won before.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: That way, they're due. It's basic math.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: So I bought 500 extra tickets with those numbers to increase my odds.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Then I realized I didn't want to win because everyone would know I'm an idiot.

jokes.text: 'Oh, sorry, guys. Sorry I'm late. I got confused and took a shower after I got dressed, because I'm Jerry.'
jokes.setup: Tom launches into a mocking impression of Jerry
jokes.punchline: The 'because I'm Jerry' tagline — delivered as self-aware confession — is the comedic apex of the impression
jokes.explanation: Tom's impression works because 'because I'm Jerry' functions as a perfect punchline — it's both cruel and economical. The specific detail (showering after dressing) is absurd but plausible for Jerry.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Did you hear about that children's entertainer who overdosed?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, no. Who?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Actually, I was wrong. It wasn't an overdose. It was Alfredo.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Alfredo the puppet. He drowned in a vat of his own sauce.

jokes.text: David Meyers, the Jewish guy who works at City Hall, once told me something. A 'schlemiel' is the guy who spills soup. A 'schlimazel' is the guy he spills it on. Jerry is both.
jokes.setup: Leslie explains Yiddish terms for types of unlucky people
jokes.punchline: Jerry is uniquely both — the clumsy person and the victim of his own clumsiness simultaneously
jokes.explanation: A smart, well-structured confessional joke. The schlemiel/schlimazel distinction is already a cultural touchstone (Laverne & Shirley), and applying both to Jerry as a unified concept is genuinely clever. Leslie's attribution to 'the Jewish guy who works at City Hall' is a small character comedy touch — she can't remember his name but specifies his religion.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Where's Jerry?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Probably in the bathroom. Again.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: What is it with him and toilets?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't ask questions I don't want answered.

jokes.text: 'And then I put my underwear on my head instead of my butt.'
jokes.setup: The office is swapping Jerry impression stories
jokes.punchline: April's contribution is a non-sequitur Jerry impression that escalates the absurdity
jokes.explanation: Functional escalation within the impression riff, but not as sharp as Tom's material. Works as a quick laugh amid the pile-on.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I can't go to the meeting, I just got dressed.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm gonna shower now.

jokes.text: Okay. Okay, guys. That's enough. / Unless somebody has another good one.
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to stop the Jerry mockery out of nominal decency
jokes.punchline: She immediately invites more if someone has something good — abandoning her own moral stance in one breath
jokes.explanation: This is a wonderfully constructed character moment. Leslie's earnest attempt at decency collapses instantly under her own morbid curiosity. The pivot happens in the same breath — 'that's enough... unless' — with perfect comic timing. It reveals Leslie's fundamental contradiction (she cares about people AND she finds the Jerry jokes irresistible) in two lines. High craft score is justified by the economy and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: A schlemiel is someone who's always getting into accidents. A schlimazel is someone who always has bad luck. And Jerry? Jerry is both.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: He's a schlemiel-schlimazel. He trips and falls into a hole, and somehow the hole was already there because of something he did last week.

jokes.text: Is that code for some kind of weird sex act? / Lord Sheldon is my dog.
jokes.setup: Jerry explains he was walking 'Lord Sheldon' when mugged
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately interprets the aristocratic dog name as a sex act euphemism
jokes.explanation: Reliable comedic structure — innuendo misunderstanding — but fairly predictable. Gets double laughs when 'Lord Sheldon' is confirmed to be the dog's actual name, which is its own absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. So you're telling me that the thing you wear on your feet is called a 'shoe'? Like, one shoe?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Yes, Tom, that's what a shoe is.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: But then what do you call it when you have two of them?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Shoes. Plural.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's the dumbest thing I've ever heard. Why would you make the plural the same as the singular? That's not how English works.

jokes.text: My wife named him. / Ew!
jokes.setup: Jerry clarifies Lord Sheldon is his dog and his wife named him
jokes.punchline: Tom's 'Ew!' is now directed at the wife's taste, not a sex act — a recycled disgust that lands differently
jokes.explanation: The callback 'Ew!' repurposed after clarification is a clean secondary beat. Tom's contempt for Jerry's entire domestic life (wife naming the dog) is a nice character extension.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, everyone, I need to say something. Jerry is a valued member of this department, and I think we should all show him some respect.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: He works hard, he's dedicated, and frankly, it's not his fault that he's a walking disaster.

jokes.text: How did you counter-attack? Fist to the throat? Did you hit him in the beanbag? There's no shame in attacking a criminal's beanbag.
jokes.setup: Tom asks Jerry how he fought back against his muggers
jokes.punchline: 'Beanbag' as a euphemism for groin, and 'there's no shame in attacking a criminal's beanbag' delivered as genuine advice
jokes.explanation: The repetition of 'beanbag' and the earnest endorsement ('there's no shame') elevates this above a simple vulgar joke. Tom's genuine investment in fighting strategy is funny. Also sets up the callback later when Andy says 'punch to the balls.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Jerry, are you okay? What happened?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I'm fine, I just tripped on the—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben! BEN! Call an ambulance! Jerry's dying!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, he's standing up.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: He's in shock, Ben! Jerry, don't listen to him, you're in shock!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I really am okay—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And now he's in denial! This is worse than I thought!

jokes.text: No, I just curled up and laid still until they left. / Well, that's another way to play it.
jokes.setup: Everyone expects Jerry to have some kind of response to his mugging; Tom has outlined fight strategies
jokes.punchline: Jerry played dead; Leslie's 'that's another way to play it' is the most diplomatic possible response to total passivity
jokes.explanation: Leslie's diplomatic understatement is pitch-perfect. 'That's another way to play it' is a gem of a line — it's supportive, accurate, and quietly devastating. Strong character integration for both characters: Jerry's haplessness and Leslie's relentless positivity.

jokes.text: Did any of them have weird tattoos or scars? If even one of them had a unique scar, we got them.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to help Jerry identify his attackers
jokes.punchline: Her detective logic is wildly overconfident — 'one unique scar and we got them' — as if this is a crime procedural
jokes.explanation: Leslie's overconfident problem-solving voice applied to an absurdly thin lead is a consistent comedic device for her character. Competent but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. Lord Sheldon? What is that?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: It's my dog.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh my God. I don't want to hear about that.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: What? He's a rescue. I named him after Sheldon Cooper.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Still don't want to hear it.

jokes.text: I feel like we're responsible for this. / Why? We didn't mug Jerry. / Well, why was he in the park? Because we tricked him into going. I don't see the connection.
jokes.setup: Leslie feels guilty; a colleague points out they didn't literally mug Jerry
jokes.punchline: The colleague follows the logic of 'we tricked him into going' to 'I don't see the connection' — willfully missing the point
jokes.explanation: The logic-defying 'I don't see the connection' after clearly stating the causal chain is a solid bit of willful obtuseness. Clean dialogue construction.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So Jerry, you know self-defense?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Well, I've taken a few classes...

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, so if someone attacks you, what do you do?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I... I try to get away.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Right, but like, what if they're coming at you with a knife?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I'd run.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What if they're coming at you with a knife AND they're on roller skates?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I... I don't know.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What if they're on roller skates and they're also on fire?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Andy, I don't think—

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: And they've got like five knives, and they're screaming about burritos? Well, the only way to defend yourself is to grab them by the beanbag.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: The beanbag?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know, their beanbag.

jokes.text: Wouldn't it be karma if we were the ones that got mugged? / Yeah. That's how pathetic Jerry is. He can't even get karma right.
jokes.setup: Leslie suggests Jerry's mugging is karma for tricking him; someone points out karma would mean THEY get mugged
jokes.punchline: Tom reframes it as Jerry being too pathetic to even attract correct karma
jokes.explanation: This is a standout joke. The philosophical escalation — karma logic applied to Jerry — arrives at 'he can't even get karma right' which is both cruel and genuinely clever. It's an original comedic construction: using correct logical analysis of karma to produce an even more devastating insult. Tom's voice is perfect here. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: A guy came up to me on the street and said 'Give me your wallet.' So I just gave it to him.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, I guess that's one way to handle it.

jokes.text: Our friend got mugged this morning. And we will not let that happen in vain. / He doesn't have a black eye. / Well, frankly, the whole department has a black eye.
jokes.setup: Leslie gives a rallying speech; someone correctly notes Jerry doesn't literally have a black eye
jokes.punchline: Leslie pivots to the metaphorical 'black eye' with total confidence, as if this was her plan all along
jokes.explanation: Leslie's rhetorical flexibility — catching a literal misreading and pivoting to metaphor without missing a beat — is consistent with her character. Clean structure, well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry, I need you to describe the person who hit your car.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Well, he was tall. Or maybe average height. I'm not great with heights.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, anything else? Hair color?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Could've been brown. Or black. Or possibly blonde. It was hard to tell with the sun.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It was 9 PM, Jerry!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I'm sorry. Are you okay? Do you need anything?

jokes.text: I have some folders. Inside are some assignments. And some homemade taffy.
jokes.setup: Leslie presents official folders for a crisis response
jokes.punchline: She casually mentions homemade taffy tucked in alongside official assignments
jokes.explanation: Perfect Leslie detail. The homemade taffy in a crisis folder is unexpected and completely in character — she bakes for her team even when mobilizing them. The flat delivery and the 'Mmm' responses make it land. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You think this is karma? For how we treat Jerry?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, Jerry's so pathetic that he absorbs other people's karma. He's like a karma sponge. We've been mean to him for years, so he's probably carrying around all of our negative energy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's not how karma works.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Well, nothing about Jerry makes sense, so why should his karma?

jokes.text: So, when you say that you want me to check in with the police liaison, you mean hook up with him, right? / No. Just check in.
jokes.setup: Leslie assigns April to check in with the police liaison
jokes.punchline: April immediately assumes 'check in' is a euphemism for hooking up with him
jokes.explanation: A quick April character beat — her deadpan nihilism toward work tasks is consistent. Not especially inventive but executed cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We can't let what happened to me be in vain. This mugging has to mean something. We have to turn this tragedy into action.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, so we're gonna catch the guy who mugged you?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, Tom. Metaphorically. We're going to fight back against crime in this city.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh. Because I was about to say, the police are already doing that.

jokes.text: We certainly are a bunch of weaklings. Especially Tom. / I am not a weakling. / Arm wrestle me right now.
jokes.setup: Ron singling out Tom as especially weak during self-defense class proposal
jokes.punchline: Tom's immediate challenge to arm wrestle exposes his fragile masculinity
jokes.explanation: Ron's casual cruelty and Tom's immediate overreaction is a reliable dynamic. The physical comedy of the arm wrestle is implied and reinforced by what follows.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We need to make this mugging symbolic of something bigger. A cautionary tale about the dangers of Pawnee.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I appreciate that, Leslie, but I'm just a guy who got mugged.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Exactly! You're the everyman. The symbol of our city's vulnerability.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: So what does that make me?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're the face of failure, Jerry. The living, breathing emblem of what's wrong with Pawnee.

jokes.text: Tom is visibly losing the arm wrestle while counting 'Three, four, five...' and the stranger walks in
jokes.setup: Tom challenged an arm wrestle to prove he's not weak
jokes.punchline: He is clearly losing, counting the seconds while his arm is being pushed down, as Ann arrives
jokes.explanation: The visual payoff of Tom counting while losing confirms the earlier joke. The interruption by Ann entering mid-struggle is good structural timing. Works better visually than on the page.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: So you want me to go through all the old Parks Department files and organize them by date?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes, exactly. It's a big project, but I know you can handle it.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: And this doesn't involve me seducing anyone?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No. Why would it?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I don't know. Seemed like all your assignments lately have been about getting people together or going on romantic adventures.

jokes.text: The black guy with the Looney Tunes ties? I love him. / No. Jerry who works with Leslie. / That Jerry? / He got mugged? / Oh. Well, I mean, that's kind of a bummer, too.
jokes.setup: Ann is told Jerry was mugged and reacts with concern
jokes.punchline: She initially thinks they mean a different Jerry (the Looney Tunes tie guy she loves), and upon the clarification it's THAT Jerry, she visibly downshifts her concern to 'kind of a bummer, too'
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured. The 'other Jerry' — identifiable only by his Looney Tunes ties, whom Ann apparently loves — creates a perfect reversal. When clarified to office Jerry, 'kind of a bummer, too' is both funny and revealing about how little Jerry is regarded. 'Looney Tunes ties' as a character descriptor is inspired. Strong episode standout.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You're all weaklings.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm a weakling? I challenge you to an arm-wrestling match right now.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You're on.

jokes.text: Scrotation Marks. / I don't know what you're talking about, but my gut says no. / New band name.
jokes.setup: Andy casually floats a band name idea to Ann
jokes.punchline: Ann's instinctive revulsion before even understanding what it is — 'my gut says no' — is the punchline
jokes.explanation: The name 'Scrotation Marks' is filthy but clever (scrotum + quotation marks). Ann's reaction — visceral disgust before understanding — is funnier than any direct response could be. 'My gut says no' is highly quotable. Andy's band name subplot is a reliable source of creative absurdity in this show.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I can take you. I've been working out.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Alright.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: One. Two. Three.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You know, I've been thinking about getting into woodworking. Four. Five.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Really focus on hand-crafted furniture. Six. Seven.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Eight. Nine. Ten.

jokes.text: Because 'Mouse Rat,' it's a great name, but at the same time, it sucks. So I think we have to change it just one more time.
jokes.setup: Andy explains his reasoning for abandoning 'Mouse Rat'
jokes.punchline: His genuine ambivalence about a name he acknowledges is great but also 'sucks' — and the eternal 'just one more time' — is pure Andy
jokes.explanation: Mouse Rat is a running band-name gag across the series. Andy's self-contradictory logic ('it's great but sucks') and eternal optimism about changing it 'one more time' is perfect characterization. Works better for fans of the show than newcomers.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Wait, which Jerry are we talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Jerry Gergich. From the Parks Department.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Oh! I thought you meant Jerry Garcia.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: No, our Jerry.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Yeah, I know. I just... Jerry Garcia is a lot more popular.

jokes.text: How are people going to become fans if they literally don't know the name of the band they're listening to? / That is a really good point.
jokes.setup: Ann advises Andy to stop changing the band name
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately agrees with the argument against his own behavior, apparently encountering this logic for the first time
jokes.explanation: Andy's genuine revelation at obvious logic — 'that is a really good point' — is a consistent character beat that plays well. His enthusiasm for agreeing is funnier than any pushback.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Oh, Jerry.

jokes.text: He's like a baby in a straightjacket.
jokes.setup: Ann describes Andy being helpless and needy in a confessional
jokes.punchline: 'Baby in a straightjacket' — completely helpless but also somehow additionally restrained
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly economical simile. A baby is already helpless; a straightjacket adds a second layer of helplessness that is both absurd and somehow logically perfect for Andy. 'Baby in a straightjacket' is instantly quotable and vivid. Strong original image that sticks in the mind.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What about 'The Awesome Possum'?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Ooh! 'Baby in a Straightjacket.' That's a good band name. I should tell him that.
jokes.setup: Ann uses 'baby in a straightjacket' as an insult about Andy in her confessional
jokes.punchline: She immediately recognizes it would make a good band name — and considers telling the person she just insulted
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke. Ann catches herself mid-insult, pivots to the band name subplot, and commits to the idea of telling Andy — her ex whom she just called helpless — a good band name she inadvertently coined while criticizing him. The self-aware meta-loop (insult → band name idea → plan to share with subject of insult) is perfectly constructed in one breath. Exceptional economy and originality. Deserves 8.5+ because it simultaneously pays off two running threads while being completely spontaneous.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Wait, your band is called Scarecrow Boat? How is that a good name?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What? It's awesome!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Andy, nobody's going to search for 'Scarecrow Boat' on the internet.

jokes.text: Ha-ha, guys. Really funny. Where's the real banner?
jokes.setup: Jerry returns to a 'Welcome Back' banner made in an hour
jokes.punchline: Jerry assumes there's a better banner — implying the visible one is clearly shoddy
jokes.explanation: Works as a visual gag (the terrible banner) with Jerry's deflated expectation. The 'we only had an hour / so did I, look what I did' exchange adds another beat revealing Leslie's compulsive over-achievement.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Andy is like a baby in a straightjacket. He doesn't know what's happening, he has no control over the situation, and he's definitely going to hurt himself.

jokes.text: He needs a lot of support. / Tom. / Talking about a bra for a man.
jokes.setup: Leslie tells the team Jerry 'needs a lot of support' emotionally
jokes.punchline: Tom reinterprets 'support' as a male bra (a 'bro/mansiere' style joke)
jokes.explanation: A reliable but low-creativity wordplay joke. The 'bra for a man' riff has been done many times (most famously Seinfeld's 'bro'). Gets the job done but doesn't add much. Tom immediately correcting himself ('Okay, seriously...') suggests even the writers knew it was a placeholder.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You're such a doofus.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Wait, that would be a great band name.

jokes.text: Wait a minute. No. That is not the graph. That's a picture from my vacation to Muncie.
jokes.setup: Jerry is giving a presentation and accidentally shows the wrong slide
jokes.punchline: His vacation photo — from Muncie, Indiana — is on the screen instead of his work graph
jokes.explanation: Jerry's haplessness in the presentation is escalating comedy — each mistake compounds. The Muncie detail is the key comedic element here, setting up the next beat.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: What is this?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I made you a banner too. I had the same amount of time as everyone else.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Look how professional it is.

jokes.text: You went on a vacation and you chose Muncie, Indiana? / Yeah. My wife and I have a time-share. / In Muncie? / Tom, Muncie is a lovely city.
jokes.setup: Jerry vacationed in Muncie, Indiana — a gloriously mundane destination
jokes.punchline: Tom's disbelief escalates, and Leslie defends Muncie with Midwest earnestness
jokes.explanation: The Muncie detail is perfect mid-America comedy. Tom's repeated disbelief ('In Muncie?') and Leslie's sincere defense is a character contrast that works. The joke reveals both Jerry's contentment with modest pleasures and Leslie's civic boosterism.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Thank you all so much for the banner. It means a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, we wanted to do something special for you, Jerry. You know, really go the extra mile.

jokes.text: We all know that it's already closed season on 'twout.'
jokes.setup: Jerry is giving a presentation about hunting and fishing seasons
jokes.punchline: He mispronounces 'trout' as 'twout' in an official context
jokes.explanation: 'Twout' is a memorable malapropism that becomes the episode's closing callback. The slip is funny and the word 'twout' itself has an inherent comedy to its sound.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry needs our support right now.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, he definitely needs a bra.

jokes.text: My marbles are full of mouth today.
jokes.setup: Jerry tries to explain his mispronunciation with the idiom 'mouth full of marbles'
jokes.punchline: He reverses the idiom entirely — 'my marbles are full of mouth' — which somehow makes less sense but more comedic sense
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The idiom reversal ('my marbles are full of mouth') is both a perfect characterization of Jerry's fumbling ineptitude AND a genuinely funny linguistic accident that sounds almost correct before your brain catches it. The confusion it would cause in the audience — did he say that? — is exactly right. Extremely quotable and original. The best verbal joke in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Okay, everyone, if I could just get this projector to work...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry, you've been standing there for five minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I know, I know, just... there we go!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Oh no, the laptop's not... it's not connecting.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Did you try turning it off and on again?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I don't know what that means.

jokes.text: Has anybody seen my glasses? I don't even think I can...
jokes.setup: Jerry's presentation has already gone wrong multiple times
jokes.punchline: He now can't find his glasses — another layer of malfunction, trailing off before even completing the sentence
jokes.explanation: Part of the escalating disaster of Jerry's presentation. Each failure compounds the last. The trailing off is a good comic beat — he can't even finish his own admission of inability.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, you went to Muncie, Indiana for vacation?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: It's a beautiful place!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Actually, Muncie has a rich history. It was a center of American manufacturing and—

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Leslie, it's Muncie. There's nothing there.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: My wife and I had a wonderful time at the Radisson.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Of course you did.

jokes.text: Is it hot in here? I feel hot. Are you guys hot? / How you guys doing? I'm good. You guys got any snacks?
jokes.setup: Leslie and Tom arrive to meet Carl, the head of park security — presumably a capable, serious professional
jokes.punchline: Carl is immediately hyperactive, distracted, and asks for snacks — completely undermining any professional authority
jokes.explanation: Carl's introduction is a good character establishment joke — he's clearly not a serious park ranger. The rapid-fire scattered questions build his chaotic energy effectively.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I meant to say 'paradigm,' not 'parody-dime.' It's a common... um... misconstrual.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Did you just make up another word?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: No, I said it perfectly. You're all just not listening with your ear-holes.

jokes.text: Carl explains he never saw Avatar because he wanted to read the book first, then realized there's no book version.
jokes.setup: Carl is delivering a talking-head confessional about being an outdoorsman
jokes.punchline: His Avatar logic — waiting for the book of a film — reveals spectacular dimness
jokes.explanation: The Avatar bit is a great character joke — his self-imposed rule (always read the book first) applied to a movie, and then the casual realization there's no book, delivered without any embarrassment. Carl's obliviousness is consistent and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: Yeah, so I've been thinking about the budget proposal, and I got some ideas, but first let me tell you about this dream I had where I was a pelican, and I could fly, but my wings kept getting tangled in spaghetti...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Carl, we really need to focus on the actual numbers here.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: Right, right, yeah. So the numbers... they're like, really big, right? Some of them have commas in them. I don't trust commas. Who decided that commas go in numbers? It's weird.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Is he okay?

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: I'm great! I'm excellent. Hey, did you guys know that mayonnaise is an instrument? Wait, no, that's not right...

jokes.text: I was wearing a t-shirt that said 'Kiss me, I'm Irish.' But no one would kiss me.
jokes.setup: Carl is sharing St. Patrick's Day plans — a normal social anecdote setup
jokes.punchline: The shirt didn't work. No one kissed him. He reports this as a neutral fact.
jokes.explanation: The deadpan delivery of social failure is very effective. Carl apparently expected the shirt to work and is mildly disappointed it didn't — his lack of self-awareness is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: I watched Avatar on my phone. It was terrible.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: All the blue people were squished.

jokes.text: You might not be so confident once you've walked a mile in my size sevens. / Kind of small feet. / Actually, seven is the worldwide average. / Boom!
jokes.setup: Carl challenges Leslie's confidence by referencing walking in his shoes; Tom notices he has small feet
jokes.punchline: Carl confidently counters with 'seven is the worldwide average' and punctuates it with 'Boom!' — treating statistical trivia as a devastating comeback
jokes.explanation: 'Boom!' as the triumphant punctuation on a piece of shoe-size statistics is wonderfully absurd. Carl's pride in his completely neutral average feet is funny, and the 'Boom!' escalates it. Good character work — Carl is the kind of person who wins arguments with unhelpful facts.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: I tried to wear green on St. Patrick's Day once. My wife said I looked like a leprechaun that had given up on life.

jokes.text: Ron, do you think that maybe I should put Mark in a headlock? That way, I can show everyone how to escape a pervert. / In the scenario you just laid out, you're the pervert. You understand that, right?
jokes.setup: Andy suggests a self-defense demonstration using a headlock
jokes.punchline: Ron logically points out that if Andy puts someone in a headlock to show escape, Andy is the pervert in that scenario
jokes.explanation: Ron's logical clarity cutting through Andy's muddy thinking is one of their best dynamics. 'You're the pervert. You understand that, right?' — the 'you understand that, right?' tag is perfectly condescending and Ron. The joke is airtight in its logic and delivery. High craft score justified by the structural precision and character integration.

jokes.text: Ann's talking head: she watches Lifetime movies for self-defense tips — specifically 'How Far is Too Far Enough: The Teri Palliber Lonergan Story'
jokes.setup: Ann explains why she's attending the self-defense class
jokes.punchline: She references a Lifetime movie with an absurdly specific fake title, then describes increasingly unhinged plot details including a therapist who 'hid in her house and tried to eat her toes'
jokes.explanation: The fake Lifetime movie title is a great joke by itself — the convoluted, vaguely grammatical title is pitch-perfect parody. 'Tried to eat her toes' as a horror detail is a great specific absurdist choice. 'Also, her daughter was having sex way too young' delivered as an afterthought is a funny structural subversion. Good running parody of Lifetime movie conventions.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm not going to put Mark in a headlock. That would give him the impression that I like him.

jokes.text: April's Lifetime movie confessional: agoraphobic woman, therapist hides in her house and tries to eat her toes, daughter having sex too young — therefore, she'll take the free self-defense class.
jokes.setup: April explains why she's attending the self-defense class
jokes.punchline: The absurdly specific Lifetime movie plot (toe-eating therapist) escalates to a second subplot (daughter's sex life), then lands on the perfectly logical conclusion: 'Free self-defense class? I'm there.'
jokes.explanation: The Lifetime movie confessional is inspired comedy writing. The movie title (a parody of real Lifetime titles), the escalating lurid plot points (therapist eating toes is peak absurdism), the aside about the daughter, and then the flat conclusion 'Free self-defense class? I'm there.' — each element lands. April's deadpan through all of it is perfect character work. High craft justified.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I've watched a lot of Lifetime movies. I know things. Like, if a woman suddenly inherits a bakery in a small town right before Christmas, she's going to fall in love with the guy who runs the general store. He'll have a daughter from a previous relationship, and there will be a big misunderstanding at the Christmas pageant, but they'll work it out by the time they're decorating gingerbread houses together.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Also, if a woman books a spa weekend and the spa is actually a front for an international diamond smuggling ring run by her estranged twin sister, she's going to have to use her pilates instructor skills as a weapon.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: And if a woman wins a trip to an all-inclusive resort, the resort owner will turn out to be her college sweetheart who faked his own death to start a new life, and she'll have to decide between her current fiancé and this guy who's now also engaged to the resort's activities coordinator.

jokes.text: I don't know, Leslie. I'd rather be back at the office. / I know this is painful for you, Jerry, but you have to be strong.
jokes.setup: Leslie has brought Jerry to the park where he was supposedly mugged, for investigation
jokes.punchline: Leslie interprets Jerry's reluctance as trauma, when in fact he knows he wasn't mugged — dramatic irony about the secret he's keeping
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony here (we don't yet know the truth, but Jerry does) creates a layered comedy on rewatch when the real reason for his reluctance is revealed. In the moment it plays as Jerry being coddled; in retrospect it's much funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That was amazing! You're like a ninja!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Thanks, Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, now let's work on your upper body strength.

jokes.text: Carl's park ranger confessional: parents made him hang out in the backyard as a kid and run around until he got tired. 'But if there's any criminals out there watching, I never get tired.'
jokes.setup: Carl claims to have 'always been a bit of an outdoorsman'
jokes.punchline: His outdoor experience is his parents making him play outside; he then issues a menacing but unconvincing warning to criminals watching a confessional
jokes.explanation: Two jokes in one: the deflation of 'outdoorsman' to 'my parents made me go outside,' then the absurdist threat to criminals through a documentary talking head. The presumption that criminals are watching and being deterred is Carl's oblivious grandiosity at its best.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: I found this log full of worms and I named it Carl Junior because it's a smaller version of me.

jokes.text: And ladies, too.
jokes.setup: Carl's threatening confessional about never getting tired
jokes.punchline: He appends 'And ladies, too' as a sort of romantic addendum to his threat — blurring menace and flirtation
jokes.explanation: A perfect tag. Three words that completely reframe the previous joke. Carl's territorial warning to criminals becoming a seduction invitation to women — separated only by a scene cut — is brilliantly economical. 'And ladies, too.' is one of the episode's most quotable moments. The economy score of 10 is warranted: maximum comedic payload per word.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: I grew up in a very small town. My father left when I was three days old. My mother worked two jobs just to keep a roof over our heads. We didn't have much, but we had each other.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: Now I'm basically a warrior. I can hunt, I can fish, I can fight. I'm very strong.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: You know, you have very nice skin. Has anyone ever told you that?

jokes.text: The first cart got pushed into the creek by kids. The second one, raccoons got onto. There was urine everywhere. The third one was recently stolen. / What's this one? / This is the second one. / The raccoon piss one.
jokes.setup: Carl explains the history of park maintenance carts
jokes.punchline: Each cart has a worse fate; the one they're using is the raccoon-urine cart, which Tom names with flat disgust
jokes.explanation: The escalating fate of three carts is well-constructed, with each worse than the last. Tom's 'The raccoon piss one' as a flat confirmation is the ideal reaction beat — he doesn't overplay it, just names it. Good escalation structure.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: We've been having some equipment problems at the Parks Department.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What kind of problems?

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: Well, our main equipment cart got damaged, so we've been using the backup cart.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The backup cart? That should be fine.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, that one got soaked in urine.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? How did that happen?

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: A raccoon got into it last week. So now we're using the second backup cart.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, and what's wrong with that one?

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: That's the urine-soaked one we're currently using.

jokes.text: Oh, no. I think we've got too much weight. / That's Tom, probably.
jokes.setup: The cart is struggling under weight; Carl assesses
jokes.punchline: Carl immediately and matter-of-factly blames Tom — not checking, not considering, just certain it's Tom
jokes.explanation: A quick character beat — Carl's casual dismissiveness about Tom is consistent with his established personality. The certainty without checking is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Carl, this cart is too heavy. Someone needs to get off and run alongside.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: I'll do it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, no. Tom, you should probably—

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. Why me?

jokes.text: Tom is told to run alongside the cart instead of riding, and he has to jog to keep up
jokes.setup: Carl determines Tom is too heavy for the cart and ejects him
jokes.punchline: Tom has to run alongside — a humiliating reversal of his expected comfort
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy derived from the situation. Tom's mortification at being the one who has to run is consistent with his vanity. Works better visually.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Andy, I'm going to demonstrate a proper chokehold on you.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. Ron, I don't think you should do that to me. You could really hurt yourself.

jokes.text: Ron puts Andy in a hold; Andy tries to escape using his neck and nearly hurts himself
jokes.setup: Ron instructs Andy to try to escape from a hold, warning he can use his legs
jokes.punchline: Andy uses his neck — the explicitly wrong body part — and nearly injures himself
jokes.explanation: Ron explicitly says 'use your legs, not your neck' — and Andy immediately uses his neck. The instructions are perfectly ironic in retrospect. This is good physical comedy that reveals Andy's instinctive wrongness.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Andy.

jokes.text: Cool. Now, I don't want to hurt you, Ron. / Don't worry about that. Just try to escape my attack. / But just promise me you'll be ready, because I mean, I don't want to destroy you.
jokes.setup: Andy is in Ron's hold and asks for permission to counter-attack
jokes.punchline: Andy's warnings to Ron — that he might 'destroy' him — while clearly at a disadvantage is peak Andy overconfidence
jokes.explanation: Andy's genuine concern that he'll hurt Ron — while Ron is effortlessly holding him — is both sweet and absurd. His 'I don't want to destroy you' is perfectly in character: he's terrifyingly incompetent but supremely self-confident.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Did you know that park rangers are assaulted more often than any other federal employee?

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: No, I didn't know that.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's a huge problem. We need to do something about it.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: Well, maybe they should stop assaulting people.

jokes.text: Can't you station a Park Ranger out here? / We have! Who do you think they're assaulting?
jokes.setup: Leslie suggests stationing a park ranger for safety
jokes.punchline: Carl reveals they already do — and the rangers are also getting assaulted
jokes.explanation: A great inverted-expectation joke with a dark edge. The structure is excellent — Leslie's solution turns out to already be in place, with the terrible consequence that the rangers are also victims. 'Who do you think they're assaulting?' as a punchline is sharp, economical, and has a genuine laugh of surprise. Strong candidate for standout moment.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Can we take a break? My feet are killing me.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: No breaks during park patrol, Tom. We need to stay vigilant.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Carl, come on. Just five minutes?

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: Tom, you're standing on a rattlesnake.

jokes.text: One way or another, I'm going to get money so you can protect Jerry, and all the other helpless, pathetic people in this town.
jokes.setup: Leslie gives a passionate speech about protecting the vulnerable
jokes.punchline: Her description of the people she wants to protect — 'helpless, pathetic' — undercuts the nobility of her mission
jokes.explanation: Leslie's well-meaning condescension is a consistent character note. She genuinely wants to help while inadvertently insulting the very people she's championing.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm sorry. That was too rough.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No, that was awesome! Teach me that move!

jokes.text: What is the first move in any fight? / Punch to the balls.
jokes.setup: Ron asks a rhetorical self-defense question; Andy gives the student answer
jokes.punchline: Andy's confident, immediate, and completely earnest answer is the most primal possible move
jokes.explanation: The callback to the beanbag discussion lands well. Andy's unironic certainty — delivered as though this is tactical genius — is perfectly in character. 'Punch to the balls' has the quality of a Ron Swanson survival tip if Ron were Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is Jerry Gergich, our Parks Department deputy director. He's incompetent, accident-prone, and somehow manages to mess up the simplest tasks on a daily basis. But he's a good friend.

jokes.text: This is my co-worker, Jerry Gergich. Diabetic. Sloppily out of shape. Friend.
jokes.setup: Leslie introduces Jerry on local TV news to publicize his mugging
jokes.punchline: Her character description of Jerry — 'Diabetic. Sloppily out of shape.' — sandwiched around 'Friend' as a final reassurance
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's peak joke. 'Diabetic. Sloppily out of shape. Friend.' — three fragments in descending propriety before 'Friend' tries to redeem the whole thing. The word 'sloppily' is inspired — it implies Jerry's lack of fitness isn't even committed. The structure (brutal assessment → warm reclaim) is perfectly Leslie: she means well but her instincts betray her constantly. Leslie inadvertently insulting people she loves while defending them is the purest expression of her character. Highly quotable, uniquely specific to this show and character.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Look, park safety is a serious issue. We need to identify the hazards and eliminate them.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: For example, we have someone who's constantly tripping over things, breaking things, and creating a mess wherever they go.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We also have someone who's always making mistakes, wasting taxpayer money, and generally being a burden on the department.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And don't even get me started on the person who shows up late, leaves early, and somehow always manages to screw things up.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So if we can just remove these hazards from the park, I think we'll see a dramatic improvement in safety.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Wait... are you talking about me?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No! ...Actually, all three of those things are kind of you.

jokes.text: He was mugged this morning in Ramsett Park. Who's next? Your frumpy uncle? Your simple neighbor? Your unpopular co-worker?
jokes.setup: Leslie appeals to the public's fear by describing vulnerable people who could be victimized
jokes.punchline: Her examples are increasingly pathetic descriptions of Jerry from different angles — frumpy uncle, simple neighbor, unpopular co-worker
jokes.explanation: Each description is technically a different type of person but is clearly also a fresh description of Jerry. 'Your simple neighbor' and 'your unpopular co-worker' are particularly cutting. The escalating characterizations while ostensibly appealing to universal sympathy is a great bit of writing.

dialogue.speaker: Paul
dialogue.line: You're being a doofus.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Hey, you can't call him that. I call him that, but you can't.

jokes.text: So, what is the solution to fix this? To make it right. And not bad.
jokes.setup: Leslie is giving a passionate TV news segment about park safety
jokes.punchline: Her call to action collapses into 'to make it right. And not bad.' — the vaguest possible advocacy
jokes.explanation: 'And not bad.' as a policy statement is beautifully absurd. Leslie's passionate advocacy melting into truistic non-commitment is both character-specific and a sharp satire of political speech.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry has a very rare condition where he can't speak in public. It's called... um... Selective Mutism Disorder.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: That's right.

jokes.text: Up next, 10 objects you didn't know you can eat.
jokes.setup: Leslie's passionate park safety segment ends
jokes.punchline: The anchor immediately pivots to a deeply weird segment — undercutting the seriousness with local news absurdity
jokes.explanation: '10 objects you didn't know you can eat' as the next segment is inspired local-news satire. Maximum economy — one line does everything. The juxtaposition with Leslie's earnest advocacy is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Well, I was walking to my car, and I tripped over the curb. Then I fell into a ditch. Then a raccoon attacked me. Then I crawled out of the ditch, and a bus hit me. Then I crawled back into the ditch to get away from the bus, and that's when I broke my leg.

jokes.text: I'm sure you'll be happy to know your little stunt worked. The Mayor is going to divert $2500 to the Parks for security upgrades.
jokes.setup: Paul (Leslie's boss) berates her for going on TV to criticize the government
jokes.punchline: Despite the scolding, it worked — and he's genuinely annoyed by this
jokes.explanation: A reliable comedic beat — the authority figure's position undermined by the success of the thing he's complaining about. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: A burrito? That's it? I once saw a guy eat a burrito so big, it required two hands and a forklift.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: That's impossible.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Not impossible. I was there. It was like that Old El Paso commercial where the girl is like 'Why not both?' Except the guy was like 'Why not all of them?' And then he died.

jokes.text: Make sure you bring the doofus who got his ass kicked. / I don't know who you're referring to. We treat everyone with respect around here.
jokes.setup: Paul instructs Leslie to bring Jerry to the announcement
jokes.punchline: Leslie's prim 'we treat everyone with respect' delivered immediately after an episode of Jerry mockery is magnificently hypocritical
jokes.explanation: Leslie's self-righteousness at the precise moment she's most implicated in Jerry's mistreatment is a great irony. Her refusal to acknowledge 'the doofus' while knowing exactly who is meant is very Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Welcome to the Shoe-shine stand! Or as I like to call it... the Shoe-Ann!

jokes.text: He can't talk right now because he has hysterical muteness from trauma. / Correct.
jokes.setup: Jerry is about to speak at the press conference to confess the truth; Leslie takes the microphone
jokes.punchline: Leslie invents 'hysterical muteness from trauma' as an excuse; Jerry — who can speak perfectly fine — confirms this diagnosis
jokes.explanation: The beauty of this joke is Jerry saying 'Correct' — a single word that immediately disproves his hysterical muteness while confirming it. The self-defeating logic is perfect. Leslie's confident medical diagnosis is also very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: This muffin is stale.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I'm sorry! Please don't hurt me!

jokes.text: I stopped for a breakfast burrito. The farting. Yeah. And Lord Sheldon lunged at a bird, I dropped the burrito, it landed on a log in the creek. So I go to reach for it, I lose my balance, and I fall on my shoulder really weird.
jokes.setup: Jerry finally confesses the true story of how he hurt himself
jokes.punchline: The real story — falling in a creek trying to retrieve a burrito dropped by a dog — is even more embarrassing than being mugged; 'the farting' interjection makes it perfect
jokes.explanation: The true story is a masterwork of comic escalation: burrito → flatulence → dog lunging at bird → dropped burrito → creek → fall. Each element is worse and funnier. 'The farting. Yeah.' as an interjected parenthetical is exceptional — it's mentioned and immediately dismissed as though it barely deserves mention. This is the episode's big structural payoff and earns its craft score.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Andy, I'm really concerned about you. You've been so nice to April lately. Have you been taking something? Should I be checking your pupils or running some blood work?

jokes.text: Are you kidding me? Imagine what Tom would have said. / Damn, Jerry! You jumped in a creek for a burrito? What would you do for a Klondike Bar? Kill your wife?
jokes.setup: Jerry explains why he lied — he was afraid of what Tom would say
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately and enthusiastically proves Jerry's fear justified with 'Kill your wife?' as the punchline
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's top jokes. The structure is brilliant: Jerry prophesies Tom's mockery → Tom immediately, eagerly, and perfectly fulfills that prophecy → the Klondike Bar riff escalates to 'Kill your wife?' which is shockingly dark. The callback to 'What would you do for a Klondike Bar?' is perfect pitch-black humor. Tom's enthusiasm — he clearly had this ready — makes it funnier. The moment simultaneously validates Jerry's entire deception and makes you understand why he lied. Near-perfect comedy construction.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: I have a video that proves you're lying.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: What? No, I'm not lying!

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: Interesting. Interesting. Interesting.

jokes.text: Block the opponent's punch and counter-punch to the jaw. / Shoeshine?
jokes.setup: Ron is demonstrating a self-defense move
jokes.punchline: Andy responds to a punch-to-the-jaw demonstration by offering a shoeshine — apparently he started a business between scenes
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy. 'Shoeshine?' is one word that implies Andy has completely abandoned the self-defense class to start an impromptu shoe-shining business. We don't need explanation — Andy starting random enterprises mid-activity is perfectly in character. The non sequitur landing mid-demonstration is surreal and very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: This is footage from the North Street intersection. As you can see, a man matching Jerry's description is being mugged.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: That's me!

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: Wait, there's more footage from later that evening.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: The man, now identified as Jerry Gergich, is chasing his dog Pui-Pui near Ramsett Creek.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: The dog has what appears to be a burrito in its mouth. Jerry attempts to retrieve it.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: And... he falls in the creek.

jokes.text: Ann Perkins, in the 'shoe-shouse.'
jokes.setup: Ann arrives while Andy is running his shoeshine operation
jokes.punchline: Andy greets Ann with a portmanteau of 'shoe' and 'house' — his branding for his shoeshine stand
jokes.explanation: 'Shoe-shouse' is a delightfully Andy coinage — he's branded his impromptu operation with a terrible portmanteau that he delivers with total pride. His genuine excitement at Ann visiting the 'shoe-shouse' is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Carl, I need a favor. What do you want in return?

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: Well, I don't know. What are you offering?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I could sleep with you.

jokes.text: I got you one of those veggie muffins that you're always eating. / Score. / Yeah. It tastes like a rug.
jokes.setup: April brings Andy a veggie muffin — a surprisingly thoughtful gesture
jokes.punchline: 'It tastes like a rug' — April's deadpan assessment of the food she voluntarily bought
jokes.explanation: April's character in one exchange: she does something unexpectedly kind, Andy responds with pure joy ('Score'), and she immediately undercuts the warmth with 'it tastes like a rug' — delivered flat, with no intention of being funny. 'It tastes like a rug' is an excellent simile and perfectly April. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: Avatar is overrated. The dialogue is wooden, the characters are one-dimensional, and the whole thing is just Dances with Wolves in space.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wow. Okay. That is... that is a controversial take. But you know what? I respect that. I think what Carl is saying is that we need to have more diverse opinions in Hollywood about big budget sci-fi films, and I for one think that's a conversation worth having.

jokes.text: April brings Andy a veggie muffin — character acting completely against type — and Andy declares 'It tastes like a rug'
jokes.setup: April unexpectedly shows up with a thoughtful gift for Andy after his self-defense incident
jokes.punchline: Andy tastes it and immediately says 'It tastes like a rug' — but continues eating it, implying a rug is fine
jokes.explanation: 'Tastes like a rug' is a good Andy-specific food complaint. The implicit continuation of eating it makes it funnier. April's character-against-type moment is the emotional setup that makes the joke land.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.line: I'm furious about that Avatar segment! We bumped a cat act for that!

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.line: You know what? Treat her like a dog. Roll over!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay!

jokes.text: Since when did he start doing stuff for other people? / Now I actually am worried that something happened to his brain.
jokes.setup: Ann observes April unexpectedly doing something nice for someone
jokes.punchline: Rather than being touched, Ann's immediate response is concern that April has a brain injury
jokes.explanation: Ann's medical instinct (brain injury) as the explanation for April's kindness is a great bit — it's simultaneously a character joke about April's usual awfulness and a character joke about Ann's clinical perspective. 'He' referring to April (April's gender is she but Ann might be speaking about Andy — ambiguous and slightly funnier either way).

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to destroy this video immediately. I'm not going to watch it or enjoy it or... okay, I'm watching it again.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It never gets old. Jerry failing at basic human tasks.

jokes.text: Carl, could you quietly quiet down for a second, and please tell me what is going on, quietly? Okay? In a quiet voice.
jokes.setup: Carl is loudly threatening to release embarrassing video footage of Jerry
jokes.punchline: Leslie's urgent whisper-instruction escalates the word 'quiet' three times while increasingly frantic — 'quietly quiet down... quietly... in a quiet voice'
jokes.explanation: The triple variation on 'quiet' ('quietly quiet down... quietly... in a quiet voice') is funny writing — the redundancy escalates as Leslie becomes more panicked. Her politeness even under crisis is perfectly Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Just skip the eating step entirely. Go straight to the bathroom.

jokes.text: Fine. I'll have sex with you in exchange for the tape. / That's not what I am saying. Okay?
jokes.setup: Leslie says she has a proposition for Carl regarding the embarrassing tape
jokes.punchline: Carl immediately offers to exchange sex for the tape — apparently misreading the situation entirely — while Leslie hastily clarifies
jokes.explanation: The inversion of the typical proposition scenario (usually the person with leverage proposes sex, not the person without it) is a clean subversion. Carl's complete failure to understand the normal power dynamic is consistent with his character.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: You know, I've thought about this a lot. When I retire, I'm going to have a nice little house downstate, maybe do some light woodworking, spend time with my family. And honestly? I'm gonna be happier than I've ever been.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: So all those jokes, all those years of people making fun of me at this office? It doesn't matter. Because I'll be the one laughing when I'm living my best life and you're all still here dealing with each other.

jokes.text: I finally saw Avatar and I thought it lived up to the hype. / Well, I'm not sure what that has to do with the mugging. / Uh... Leslie. Counterpoint. I disagree with Carl. I have seen Avatar as well, and I think it exceeded the hype.
jokes.setup: Carl is on TV with supposed bombshell information about the mugging case
jokes.punchline: His 'bombshell' is his Avatar opinion; Leslie, seemingly just to save the segment, offers a counterpoint — she thinks it exceeded the hype
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's most sophisticated joke. The Avatar thread (established in Carl's confessional) pays off brilliantly: Carl uses a live TV bombshell opportunity to share his Avatar review. The anchor's confused 'I'm not sure what that has to do with the mugging' is the perfect straight-man response. Then Leslie — who should know better — takes Carl's bait and offers a counterpoint about Avatar, fully committing to the absurdity. 'Disagreement. Well, things are really heating up in here' completes the bit. The callback structure, the escalation, and Leslie's complete capitulation to the absurdity make this exceptional. One of the episode's standout moments.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Hey Jerry, where do you want to go for lunch? Some kind of... gazpacho?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Gazpacho!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Gazpacho!

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Gazpacho!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: It's gazpacho...

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Gazpacho.

jokes.text: Do you know that I bumped a cat that can stand up on its hinders for you?
jokes.setup: The TV anchor/producer berates Leslie for the disastrous Avatar segment
jokes.punchline: She reveals she bumped a cat that stands on its hind legs — a sacred slot in local TV — for this segment
jokes.explanation: 'A cat that can stand up on its hinders' is inspired Pawnee local TV content. 'Hinders' as a word for hind legs is a perfect period-specific colloquialism for this character. The anchor's genuine outrage at losing this segment slot for Leslie's Avatar debacle is very funny. 'Hinders' alone earns a high quotability score.

jokes.text: I am part of a great team. And sometimes, the best way to maintain a strong team is just by letting someone know that he is still a part of it. / This is the only copy, and I am going to destroy it. / Right after I watch it one more time. / I'm sorry, but it is so good.
jokes.setup: Leslie's confessional about protecting Jerry and team loyalty; she has the embarrassing tape
jokes.punchline: Her noble declaration is immediately followed by watching the tape one more time — she can't resist — and genuinely loving it
jokes.explanation: A perfect Leslie moment. Her authentic caring speech about team loyalty collapses into 'right after I watch it one more time' — and the apologetic, helpless 'I'm sorry, but it is so good' makes it even better. She is simultaneously a great person and someone who cannot resist the comedy of Jerry's misfortune. This contradiction IS Leslie Knope, and it's executed perfectly.

jokes.text: I got you a peppermint latte. / Seriously? My goodness. I love a peppermint... / I know.
jokes.setup: Tom makes a surprise kind gesture to Jerry, who is genuinely touched
jokes.punchline: Before Jerry can complete his grateful 'I love a peppermint latte,' Tom spills it on him — returning immediately to normal
jokes.explanation: A beautiful structural joke that plays on the episode's warmth — we think Tom has genuinely turned a corner — before immediately spilling the latte. 'I know.' as the punchline is perfect: Tom knew he was going to spill it. The fakeout of genuine kindness → immediate classic Jerry treatment is earned by the episode's themes and perfectly timed.

jokes.text: We should just directly apply the food to your clothes.
jokes.setup: Tom has just spilled a latte on Jerry
jokes.punchline: A suggestion to skip the middleman entirely — just put food directly on Jerry's clothes
jokes.explanation: A sharp, economical observation that takes Jerry's food-related misfortune and reduces it to a logical efficiency proposal. 'Directly apply the food to your clothes' is a memorable line.

jokes.text: Making fun of Jerry is back!
jokes.setup: Jerry is being mocked again after a brief period of being treated with respect
jokes.punchline: Tom announces the return of mockery as though it's a beloved TV show returning from hiatus
jokes.explanation: Tom announcing 'Making fun of Jerry is back!' with genuine joy — as though it's a cultural event — is both meta (acknowledging the show's running gag) and perfectly in character. The episode-long arc of treating Jerry with respect collapses in one announcement. 'Is back!' with the implied exclamation mark is one of the episode's most memorable lines. High quotability, very strong character integration.

jokes.text: They can laugh at me all they want. Because two more years until I retire with full benefits and pension. And the wife and I, we have bought a little cottage on a lake. And I am going to get myself a stack of mystery novels, a box of cigars, and I am going to sit back and enjoy my life.
jokes.setup: Jerry's final confessional — addressed to the audience after being mocked again
jokes.punchline: Jerry has a fully realized, peaceful retirement plan that makes the mockery irrelevant — he's already won
jokes.explanation: A genuinely warm and funny final beat. Jerry's contentment — cottage, mystery novels, cigars — is specific and lovely. The comedy comes from the realization that Jerry doesn't actually need their validation; he has a rich inner life planned. It recontextualizes his tolerance of the office mockery as confidence rather than submission. This is emotionally earned comedy, not cheap laughs.

jokes.text: Hey, Jerry? April was just double-checking the lunch order. Do you want the salmon or the 'twout'? / Twout! Twout! Twout! Twout!
jokes.setup: The episode's final moment — April offers Jerry a choice referencing his earlier mispronunciation
jokes.punchline: The entire office chants 'Twout!' — the embarrassing slip from the presentation becoming a shared office ritual
jokes.explanation: The perfect episode closer. 'Twout' was established as an accidental malapropism; it's now canonized as a chant. The entire office chanting it has an infectious energy, and Jerry's warm response (from his earlier confessional, he's clearly fine with this) makes the ending both funny and strangely heartwarming. Excellent callback structure — the setup was mild but the payoff is outsized. One of the episode's standout moments.

tmdb_overview: After Jerry gets mugged by a bunch of kids, Leslie meets with the head park ranger in hopes of improving park safety. Meanwhile, everyone tries to be nicer to Jerry once he returns to the office.
insight: Safety hazard escalation drives 70 jokes in 24 minutes—Parks' densest episode yet.
